nameStory: The 'harlequin' in harlequin glorybower refers to the colorful, almost theatrical display this plant puts on - like the multicolored costume of a harlequin performer. Its flowers are fragrant white stars that give way to brilliant blue berries nestled in bright red calyxes, creating a striking two-toned show. Some folks also call it the 'peanut butter tree' because the leaves smell distinctly like peanut butter when crushed!
description: Harlequin glorybower is a deciduous shrub or small tree that can grow 10-20 feet tall, though it's often smaller in New England's climate. This Asian native has large, heart-shaped leaves and produces clusters of sweetly fragrant white flowers in late summer. The real showstopper comes in fall when the plant displays its unusual berries - bright blue fruits sitting in persistent red star-shaped calyxes that look almost artificial in their vivid coloring. Despite being in the mint family, it doesn't look like what most people think of as a 'mint plant.'

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Brilliant turquoise-blue berries nestled in bright red, star-shaped calyxes create an unmistakable two-tone display in fall - no other New England plant has this exact color combination

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large heart-shaped leaves (4-8 inches long) arranged in pairs along the stems, with a distinctive peanut butter smell when crushed or bruised

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Fragrant white flowers in flat-topped clusters appear in late summer, each flower having a tubular shape with long protruding stamens that give them a spidery appearance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Multi-stemmed shrub or small tree with somewhat open, irregular branching and smooth grayish bark

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Small, pointed buds arranged opposite each other along smooth twigs that may have a slightly square cross-section typical of mint family plants

habitat: In New England, harlequin glorybower is found as an ornamental escape or naturalized plant in disturbed areas, woodland edges, and old garden sites. It prefers well-drained soils and can tolerate both sun and partial shade. You're most likely to spot it near old homesteads or in areas where it was once cultivated and has spread on its own.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge late in spring, unfurling as soft, light green heart shapes. The plant leafs out later than many native species.
seasonality.summer: Fragrant white flower clusters appear in late summer (August-September), attracting butterflies and other pollinators with their sweet perfume.
seasonality.fall: The spectacular blue and red berry display peaks in early fall, while leaves may turn yellow before dropping. This is the easiest time to identify the plant.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the opposite branching pattern, and dried red calyxes may persist on the twigs, providing winter identification clues.

funFact: The brilliant blue color in harlequin glorybower berries comes from a pigment called trichotomine that was completely unknown to science until researchers studied this plant - it's the only place this particular blue compound has ever been found in nature!
confusionNotes: The heart-shaped leaves might be confused with catalpa or redbud trees, but neither of those produces the distinctive blue and red berries. The peanut butter smell when leaves are crushed is a dead giveaway that you've found harlequin glorybower.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name including 'glorybower,' this plant is actually in the mint family (Lamiaceae), not related to true bowers or vines. The 'glory' refers to its showy display, and many gardeners are surprised to learn their fragrant ornamental shrub is technically a mint relative.
compareHints: Japanese glorybower, the only other Clerodendrum species you might encounter in New England, has much larger leaves and different flower clusters. Harlequin glorybower's distinctive peanut butter leaf scent and the specific blue-berry-in-red-calyx combination make it easily distinguishable from other mint family members like beautyberry, which has purple berries clustered directly along the stems.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Japanese glorybower differs from its relative harlequin glorybower by having much larger, heart-shaped leaves (versus smaller oval ones) and pink-and-white flowers in dense upright clusters (versus small white flowers in looser, branched clusters).
